items.title: 90-6 and One Deadline Dodged: Inside Congress's Stopgap Deal to Avoid an October Shutdown
items.body:
With federal funding under the FY2026 appropriations calendar set to expire on September 30, Congress has once again reached for its most familiar budget tool: the continuing resolution. A bipartisan measure to keep federal agencies funded into December cleared the Senate by a lopsided 90-6 margin before moving to the House, averting an October 1 shutdown that both parties said they wanted to avoid heading into a politically sensitive stretch of the calendar.

The vote tally itself tells a story. A 90-6 outcome in a chamber known for narrow, party-line splits signals that neither side wanted its fingerprints on a shutdown this time around. But the lopsided count also masks how little the underlying disagreements have actually been resolved — a continuing resolution, by design, doesn't settle a budget fight so much as postpone it.

## What a Continuing Resolution Actually Does

A CR is a stopgap spending bill that extends current funding levels for federal agencies past the start of a new fiscal year, buying lawmakers more time to negotiate full-year appropriations bills. It doesn't set new spending priorities or resolve disputes over individual agency budgets; it simply freezes the status quo, typically with minor technical adjustments, for a set number of weeks or months.

This year's version extends funding into December, meaning the government avoids an immediate lapse but faces the same cliff again before the holidays — and, notably, just weeks before the 2026 midterm election season shifts into higher gear.

## Why December, Not Later

The choice of a December deadline wasn't accidental. It's long enough to avoid the optics of a shutdown heading into October, but short enough that leadership in both chambers retains leverage to force another round of negotiations before lawmakers leave for the holidays. Punting past the midterms entirely would have required a much longer CR — an option that reportedly drew resistance from lawmakers who worry that funding agencies on autopilot for a full year erodes Congress's power of the purse and locks in spending levels that no longer reflect current priorities.

## What Got Punted

The stopgap deal notably does not resolve several of the thornier disputes that have stalled full-year appropriations work:

- **Topline spending levels** — how much to allocate between defense and non-defense discretionary programs remains unsettled.
- **Policy riders** — provisions attached to individual spending bills that touch on regulatory and agency-specific policy questions continue to be a sticking point between the chambers.
- **Individual agency allocations** — several of the twelve annual appropriations bills have not advanced far enough to reconcile House and Senate versions.

In other words, the CR keeps the lights on without answering any of the questions that made passing full-year funding difficult in the first place.

## The Midterm Backdrop

Timing matters here. A funding fight dragging into an election year raises the stakes for both parties, since a shutdown close to voting season tends to generate outsized political blame in whichever direction voters assign it. By pushing the next deadline to December, lawmakers buy themselves a legislative session removed from the most intense phase of midterm campaigning, even as the underlying disputes — spending levels, riders, and individual agency budgets — will still need to be resolved eventually.

## What Comes Next

Federal agencies, contractors, and grant recipients now have a period of funding certainty, but it's a conditional one. Budget offices across the government will continue operating under current-year funding levels rather than any newly negotiated amounts, and agencies generally avoid launching new initiatives during CR periods due to the funding uncertainty involved.

For everyday observers, the practical takeaway is straightforward: no shutdown in October, but the same fight resumes in December, closer to the holidays and with the same unresolved questions about spending levels and policy riders still on the table. Whether that translates into a smoother resolution or another down-to-the-wire scramble will depend on how much progress negotiators make on the individual appropriations bills in the weeks ahead.

items.title: Boeing's 737 Max Output Stalls at 47 a Month, Clouding Plans to Reach 52 Next Year
items.body:
Boeing's long-promised path back to full-speed production of its best-selling jet is proving harder to walk than investors had hoped. Chief Executive Kelly Ortberg told analysts that stabilizing 737 Max output at the company's current target rate is taking longer than expected, a disclosure that sent Boeing shares lower and reignited questions about whether the planemaker can hit its next milestone: ramping up to 52 jets a month sometime next year.

## Where Production Actually Stands

Boeing has spent much of the past two years trying to climb back to a steady cadence after a mid-air door-plug blowout on an Alaska Airlines Max 9 in January 2024 prompted regulators to cap output while the company overhauled its quality-control processes. Since then, the Federal Aviation Administration has allowed Boeing to inch production upward in stages, and the company has said it is currently building around 47 Max jets a month at its Renton, Washington, plant.

The trouble, according to Ortberg, is not building more airplanes — it is building them at a consistent, repeatable pace without the fits and starts that have plagued the program for years. "Stable" has become the operative word inside Boeing's factories: the company wants to prove it can hold a rate for a sustained stretch before asking regulators for permission to go higher, rather than repeating a pattern of surges followed by slowdowns.

## Why the Ramp Keeps Slipping

A combination of factors has kept Boeing from locking in that stability. Supply-chain constraints — particularly around fuselage delivery from supplier Spirit AeroSystems, engines, and other structural components — continue to create bottlenecks that ripple through final assembly. Boeing has also been deliberately slowing its own internal pace at times to work through traveled work, the industry term for tasks left incomplete as a plane moves down the line, which regulators have flagged as a root cause of past quality lapses.

Labor availability and training have added further friction. Boeing brought on thousands of new mechanics and inspectors as part of its quality reset, and integrating that workforce while simultaneously trying to increase output has taken longer than management initially projected.

## What It Means for the 52-a-Month Target

Boeing has repeatedly pointed to 52 Max jets a month as a milestone it hopes to reach next year, a rate the company has not sustained since before the two fatal Max crashes in 2018 and 2019 that led to a 20-month grounding of the fleet. Ortberg's comments suggest that timeline could be at risk if stabilization at 47 a month takes longer than planned, since the FAA has signaled it will not approve further rate increases until Boeing demonstrates consistent performance at existing levels.

For airline customers waiting on deliveries — including major U.S. and international carriers that have restructured fleet plans around Max deliveries — a slower ramp means continued uncertainty about when backlogged orders will actually arrive. Boeing's delivery backlog for the Max numbers in the thousands of aircraft, and persistent production delays can affect airline capacity planning, aircraft leasing costs, and route expansion decisions across the industry.

## Market Reaction

Investors responded to Ortberg's remarks by pushing Boeing shares lower, reflecting concern that a slower-than-expected ramp could push out the timeline for the company to generate the free cash flow it has promised. Boeing has been working to shore up its balance sheet after years of losses tied to the Max grounding, the COVID-19 downturn in air travel, and production problems on other programs, and steady, growing deliveries of the 737 Max are central to that recovery plan.

## The Bigger Picture

Boeing's leadership has framed the slower ramp as a deliberate trade-off: prioritizing safety and quality discipline over speed, even if that means near-term financial targets slip. Whether that approach satisfies investors, airline customers, and regulators alike may depend on how quickly the company can show it has finally broken the boom-and-bust cycle that has defined 737 Max production for much of the past decade.

items.title: 58% Higher and Climbing: Inside the ACA Premium Shock Hitting Millions This Fall
items.body:
## A Sharp Jump in What Families Actually Pay

Millions of Americans who buy health insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplaces are opening their fall renewal notices to a jarring number. According to research from health policy analysts, the average monthly premium that marketplace enrollees pay after tax credits are applied has climbed from about $113 to roughly $178 — an increase of nearly 58%. For a household budget, that is not a rounding error. It is the difference between an affordable monthly bill and a genuine financial strain.

The timing lines up with open enrollment season, which typically runs from November through mid-January in most states. That means the sticker shock is landing right as households are being asked to actively choose or renew a plan for the coming year.

## Why the Cost of Coverage Is Rising

The core driver behind this increase is the scheduled expiration of enhanced federal subsidies that were first introduced during the pandemic and later extended. Those enhanced tax credits reduced out-of-pocket premium costs for a broad range of income levels, including many middle-income households that previously received little or no assistance. As those enhancements lapse, the subsidy amount shrinks, and the gap that enrollees must cover out of pocket grows — even if the sticker price of the underlying plan hasn't changed dramatically.

On top of that, insurers in many states have also filed for higher base rates for next year, citing rising medical costs, hospital and prescription drug prices, and higher utilization of care. When a smaller subsidy meets a higher list price, the combined effect on what a family actually pays can be substantial.

## Who Is Most Exposed

Health policy researchers estimate that as many as 4 million people could lose marketplace coverage in the coming year if enrollment trends continue on their current path. Early sign-up data already shows softening enrollment compared to the same point in prior years, which analysts attribute to affordability concerns and confusion around new subsidy amounts.

The households most exposed tend to be:

- **Self-employed workers and small-business owners** who rely on the individual market because they don't have access to employer coverage.
- **Early retirees** not yet eligible for Medicare who buy marketplace plans to bridge the gap.
- **Gig workers and freelancers** whose income can hover near the thresholds where subsidy eligibility changes sharply.
- **Middle-income families** who benefited from the temporary subsidy expansion but may fall outside more limited assistance going forward.

## What Experts Are Watching

Nonpartisan researchers, insurance regulators, and consumer advocacy groups are watching two things closely this fall: whether Congress takes any action on subsidy levels before enrollment locks in for next year, and how state insurance marketplaces communicate the changes to enrollees. Several state-run exchanges have said they are ramping up outreach and reminding consumers to actively shop around rather than letting a plan auto-renew, since switching to a different plan or metal tier can sometimes offset part of the increase.

Consumer advocates also note that subsidy eligibility and amounts vary significantly by income, age, family size, and state, so national averages don't tell the whole story for any individual household. A modest premium increase for one family could be a much larger jump for another, depending on exactly where their income falls relative to subsidy cutoffs.

## What Enrollees Can Do Right Now

Financial counselors and healthcare navigators generally recommend a few concrete steps as open enrollment approaches:

1. **Don't let your plan auto-renew without checking.** Log back into the marketplace and re-verify income and household information, since outdated estimates can affect your subsidy amount.
2. **Compare plans across metal tiers.** A lower-premium bronze or silver plan with a higher deductible may make more financial sense for some households than staying on last year's plan.
3. **Ask about free local help.** Certified enrollment assisters and navigators, often available through community health centers or state marketplaces, can help estimate real costs at no charge.
4. **Check state-based programs.** Some states have supplemental subsidy programs on top of federal tax credits, which can meaningfully soften the increase.

## The Bigger Picture

This year's premium jump is a reminder of how sensitive household healthcare costs are to federal policy decisions that can shift from one year to the next. Whether or not lawmakers revisit the subsidy structure, the immediate reality for many families is that the cost of maintaining coverage is going up, and open enrollment is the narrow window in which they can act to manage that increase. Financial advisors generally encourage anyone affected to review their options early rather than waiting until the final days of the enrollment period, when plan comparisons and assistance appointments become harder to schedule.
